lesson_1.topicLabel: Enquiry 01: Rainforest Kingdom — Ogiso Rulers and Red-Earth Walls (c. AD 900–1180)
lesson_1.title: How did Edo communities build a vast rainforest kingdom by AD 900?
lesson_1.spokenTitle: How did Edo communities build a vast rainforest kingdom by AD 900?

cards.heading: Ogiso Kings in Nigeria
cards.connective: How did Edo communities build a vast rainforest kingdom by AD 900?
cards.html: In southern Nigeria’s lush rainforest, Edo farmers grew yams and palm oil under early Ogiso rulers.
cards.spoken: How did Edo communities build a vast rainforest kingdom by AD 900? <short pause> In southern Nigeria’s lush rainforest, Edo farmers grew yams and palm oil under early Ogiso rulers.

cards.heading: 16,000 km of Red-Clay Iya
cards.connective: United villages worked together to dig giant earthworks by hand.
cards.html: Using iron hoes and reed baskets, teams dug deep Iya moats and sun-baked red laterite walls around 500+ towns.
cards.spoken: United villages worked together to dig giant earthworks by hand. <short pause> Using iron hoes and reed baskets, teams dug deep Iya moats and sun-baked red laterite walls around 500+ towns.

cards.heading: AD 900 Britain Contrast
cards.stat: Saxon Timber Burhs vs Giant Edo Moats
cards.connective: Meanwhile, Anglo-Saxon Britain built on a much smaller scale.
cards.html: While Anglo-Saxon monks wrote on parchment inside small timber burhs, Edo built vast walls and oral history.
cards.spoken: Meanwhile, Anglo-Saxon Britain built on a much smaller scale. <short pause> While Anglo-Saxon monks wrote on parchment inside small timber burhs, Edo built vast walls and oral history.

cards.heading: A West African Engineering Power
cards.connective: Rich forest farming and teamwork built an enduring kingdom.
cards.html: Early Edo communities turned southern Nigeria’s rainforest into one of the medieval world’s greatest earthwork kingdoms.
cards.spoken: Rich forest farming and teamwork built an enduring kingdom. <short pause> Early Edo communities turned southern Nigeria’s rainforest into one of the medieval world’s greatest earthwork kingdoms.

lesson_1.takeaway: Around AD 900 in southern Nigeria, Edo communities united under Ogiso rulers and dug 16,000 kilometres of red-clay Iya earthworks far larger than Anglo-Saxon burhs.
vocab: 1. Edo
People, language, and heartland of Benin in southern Nigeria.
2. Ogiso
Early Benin rulers whose title meant "Kings of the Sky".
3. Iya
16,000 km of red-clay ditches and banks dug around Edo towns.

lesson_1.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Around AD 900 in southern Nigeria, Edo communities united under Ogiso rulers and dug 16,000 kilometres of red-clay Iya earthworks far larger than Anglo-Saxon burhs.

lesson_2.topicLabel: Enquiry 02: From Ogiso to Oba — Ewuare the Great and Golden Benin City (c. AD 1180–1500)
lesson_2.title: How did Oba Ewuare the Great turn Benin City into a golden capital?
lesson_2.spokenTitle: How did Oba Ewuare the Great turn Benin City into a golden capital?

cards.heading: Sacred Ife to Oba Eweka I
cards.connective: How did Oba Ewuare the Great turn Benin City into a golden capital?
cards.html: Around AD 1180, Prince Oranmiyan came from sacred Ife and his son Oba Eweka I founded Benin’s Oba line.
cards.spoken: How did Oba Ewuare the Great turn Benin City into a golden capital? <short pause> Around AD 1180, Prince Oranmiyan came from sacred Ife and his son Oba Eweka I founded Benin’s Oba line.

cards.heading: Ewuare’s 9 Gates & Oil Lamps
cards.stat: Inner Moat, Drains & Night Street Lamps
cards.connective: Around 1440, Oba Ewuare the Great redesigned Edo on a grand scale.
cards.html: Oba Ewuare built nine fortified gates, straight drained avenues, and tall palm-oil lamps long before London.
cards.spoken: Around 1440, Oba Ewuare the Great redesigned Edo on a grand scale. <short pause> Oba Ewuare built nine fortified gates, straight drained avenues, and tall palm-oil lamps long before London.

cards.heading: Coral Regalia & 40 Guilds
cards.stat: Red Coral Crowns & Brass Roof Birds
cards.connective: Inside the walled palace, royal guilds created dazzling court splendour.
cards.html: Watched over by brass palace birds, Ewuare wore red coral beads, launched Igue, and backed forty craft guilds.
cards.spoken: Inside the walled palace, royal guilds created dazzling court splendour. <short pause> Watched over by brass palace birds, Ewuare wore red coral beads, launched Igue, and backed forty craft guilds.

cards.heading: West Africa’s Planned Royal City
cards.stat: Safe Gates + Clean Streets + Master Guilds
cards.connective: Strong kingship and town planning launched Benin’s Golden Age.
cards.html: From Oba Eweka I to Ewuare the Great, Benin City grew into one of the fifteenth-century world’s most orderly capitals.
cards.spoken: Strong kingship and town planning launched Benin’s Golden Age. <short pause> From Oba Eweka I to Ewuare the Great, Benin City grew into one of the fifteenth-century world’s most orderly capitals.

lesson_2.takeaway: Founded through sacred Ife under Oba Eweka I around AD 1180, Benin City was rebuilt around 1440 by Oba Ewuare with nine gates, wide avenues, palm-oil lamps, coral regalia, and forty guilds.
vocab: 1. Oba
Sacred king of the Kingdom of Benin since c. AD 1180.
2. Ife
Sacred Yoruba city north-west of Benin linked to Eweka I.
3. Dynasty
Line of kings or queens belonging to the same royal family.
lesson_2.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Ethnologisches Museum Berlin, MARKK Hamburg, MAA Cambridge, National Museum Benin City and Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_2.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Founded through sacred Ife under Oba Eweka I around AD 1180, Benin City was rebuilt around 1440 by Oba Ewuare with nine gates, wide avenues, palm-oil lamps, coral regalia, and forty guilds.

lesson_3.topicLabel: Enquiry 03: Lost-Wax Masterpieces — Igun Street Brass-Casters, Ivory and Coral (c. AD 1400–1700)
lesson_3.title: How did Igun Street artists cast brass plaques to record Benin’s history?
lesson_3.spokenTitle: How did Igun Street artists cast brass plaques to record Benin’s history?

cards.heading: Golden Brass on Igun Street
cards.connective: How did Igun Street artists cast brass plaques to record Benin’s history?
cards.html: Most Benin Bronzes were golden brass cast solely for the Oba by hereditary families on Igun Street.
cards.spoken: How did Igun Street artists cast brass plaques to record Benin’s history? <short pause> Most Benin Bronzes were golden brass cast solely for the Oba by hereditary families on Igun Street.

cards.heading: 3-Step Lost-Wax Casting
cards.connective: Sculptors turned soft yellow beeswax into solid metal masterpieces.
cards.html: Heat melted out the carved beeswax model, casters poured brass from a clay crucible, and cool clay was cracked open.
cards.spoken: Sculptors turned soft yellow beeswax into solid metal masterpieces. <short pause> Heat melted out the carved beeswax model, casters poured brass from a clay crucible, and cool clay was cracked open.

cards.heading: Plaques & Carved Ivory Tusks
cards.connective: Brass and ivory worked side by side as Benin’s royal memory.
cards.html: Plaques nailed onto wooden palace pillars and carved ivory tusks recorded kings, warriors, and visitors.
cards.spoken: Brass and ivory worked side by side as Benin’s royal memory. <short pause> Plaques nailed onto wooden palace pillars and carved ivory tusks recorded kings, warriors, and visitors.

cards.heading: Master West African Bronze Casters
cards.connective: Every cracked mould revealed a one-of-a-kind royal treasure.
cards.html: Benin’s Igun Street brass-casters and ivory-carvers created one of humanity’s greatest artistic archives.
cards.spoken: Every cracked mould revealed a one-of-a-kind royal treasure. <short pause> Benin’s Igun Street brass-casters and ivory-carvers created one of humanity’s greatest artistic archives.

lesson_3.takeaway: Centuries before European contact, Benin’s royal guild on Igun Street used beeswax-and-clay lost-wax casting to create over 900 brass plaques and royal heads alongside carved ivory tusks.
vocab: 1. Benin Bronzes
Royal Benin sculptures mostly cast from bright golden brass.
2. Brass
Golden metal alloy of copper and zinc used on Igun Street.
3. Igun Street
Royal street in Benin City home to master brass-casters.
lesson_3.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Ethnologisches Museum Berlin, MARKK Hamburg, MAA Cambridge, National Museum Benin City and Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_3.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Centuries before European contact, Benin’s royal guild on Igun Street used beeswax-and-clay lost-wax casting to create over 900 brass plaques and royal heads alongside carved ivory tusks.

lesson_4.topicLabel: Enquiry 04: Sacred Court Rituals — The Oba, Queen Mother Idia and Everyday Edo Life (c. AD 1500–1700)
lesson_4.title: What was life like inside the Oba’s court and Edo rainforest villages?
lesson_4.spokenTitle: What was life like inside the Oba’s court and Edo rainforest villages?

cards.heading: Leopard & Mudfish Symbols
cards.connective: What was life like inside the Oba’s court and Edo rainforest villages?
cards.html: Spotted leopards showed the Oba’s rule on land, while coiled mudfish linked him to sea-god Olokun.
cards.spoken: What was life like inside the Oba’s court and Edo rainforest villages? <short pause> Spotted leopards showed the Oba’s rule on land, while coiled mudfish linked him to sea-god Olokun.

cards.heading: Oba Esigie & Iyoba Idia
cards.connective: Strong female wisdom helped steer Benin’s sixteenth-century Golden Age.
cards.html: Oba Esigie honoured his wise mother Idia as first Iyoba with Uselu palace and a carved ivory mask.
cards.spoken: Strong female wisdom helped steer Benin’s sixteenth-century Golden Age. <short pause> Oba Esigie honoured his wise mother Idia as first Iyoba with Uselu palace and a carved ivory mask.

cards.heading: Edo Farms, Cloth & Igue
cards.connective: Beyond palace walls, hardworking villages sustained the whole kingdom.
cards.html: Families in red-clay compounds grew white yams, wove cotton cloth, and danced at the annual Igue festival.
cards.spoken: Beyond palace walls, hardworking villages sustained the whole kingdom. <short pause> Families in red-clay compounds grew white yams, wove cotton cloth, and danced at the annual Igue festival.

cards.heading: Harmony Across Palace and Village
cards.connective: Prosperous farms and guilds made Benin ready for global trade.
cards.html: Golden Age Benin united Oba Esigie, Queen Mother Idia, and thriving rainforest villages into one proud society.
cards.spoken: Prosperous farms and guilds made Benin ready for global trade. <short pause> Golden Age Benin united Oba Esigie, Queen Mother Idia, and thriving rainforest villages into one proud society.

lesson_4.takeaway: Under Oba Esigie and wise Queen Mother Idia, Benin blended sacred court rituals honouring Olokun and royal ancestors with thriving villages growing yams, palm oil, and cotton cloth.
vocab: 1. Iyoba
Royal title of Queen Mother created for wise Idia.
2. Olokun
Edo god of rivers, seas, wealth, and good fortune.
3. Mudfish
Fish able to cross damp mud, linking land and sea-god Olokun.
lesson_4.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Ethnologisches Museum Berlin, MARKK Hamburg, MAA Cambridge, National Museum Benin City and Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_4.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Under Oba Esigie and wise Queen Mother Idia, Benin blended sacred court rituals honouring Olokun and royal ancestors with thriving villages growing yams, palm oil, and cotton cloth.

lesson_5.topicLabel: Enquiry 05: Global Traders — Brass Manillas, Cowrie Shells and European Visitors (c. AD 1485–1850)
lesson_5.title: Why were European visitors so amazed by Benin’s trade and wide streets?
lesson_5.spokenTitle: Why were European visitors so amazed by Benin’s trade and wide streets?

cards.heading: 1485 Ships & Lisbon Envoys
cards.connective: Why were European visitors so amazed by Benin’s trade and wide streets?
cards.html: After Portuguese ships reached Gwato port in 1485, Benin set prices, sent Lisbon ambassadors, and spoke Portuguese.
cards.spoken: Why were European visitors so amazed by Benin’s trade and wide streets? <short pause> After Portuguese ships reached Gwato port in 1485, Benin set prices, sent Lisbon ambassadors, and spoke Portuguese.

cards.heading: Manillas & Cowrie Money
cards.connective: Ocean trade poured fresh metal into Igun Street’s furnaces.
cards.html: Swapping Benin pepper and cloth brought market cowrie shells and brass manillas melted into palace plaques!
cards.spoken: Ocean trade poured fresh metal into Igun Street’s furnaces. <short pause> Swapping Benin pepper and cloth brought market cowrie shells and brass manillas melted into palace plaques!

cards.heading: Olfert Dapper’s 1668 Praise
cards.connective: Dutch merchant diaries amazed readers across seventeenth-century Europe.
cards.html: In 1668, Olfert Dapper praised Benin’s thirty straight streets, polished clay walls, and Haarlem-sized palace.
cards.spoken: Dutch merchant diaries amazed readers across seventeenth-century Europe. <short pause> In 1668, Olfert Dapper praised Benin’s thirty straight streets, polished clay walls, and Haarlem-sized palace.

cards.heading: West Africa’s Proud Trading Power
cards.connective: For four centuries, Benin traded on its own royal rules.
cards.html: Pre-colonial Benin regulated European ships, turned imported manillas into art, and maintained model avenues.
cards.spoken: For four centuries, Benin traded on its own royal rules. <short pause> Pre-colonial Benin regulated European ships, turned imported manillas into art, and maintained model avenues.

lesson_5.takeaway: From 1485, the Oba regulated foreign ships at Gwato port, melted imported brass manillas into plaques, and impressed Europe in Olfert Dapper’s 1668 account of Benin’s thirty wide streets.
vocab: 1. Gwato Port
Benin River port where ships sought the Oba’s trade licence.
2. Ambassador
Official royal envoy sent to represent a king abroad.
3. Manillas
Horseshoe-shaped brass bracelets melted down for plaques.
lesson_5.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Ethnologisches Museum Berlin, MARKK Hamburg, MAA Cambridge, National Museum Benin City and Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_5.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> From 1485, the Oba regulated foreign ships at Gwato port, melted imported brass manillas into plaques, and impressed Europe in Olfert Dapper’s 1668 account of Benin’s thirty wide streets.

lesson_6.topicLabel: Enquiry 06: 1897 British Invasion, Looted Bronzes and Living Edo Heritage Today (1897–Present)
lesson_6.title: Why did Britain invade Benin in 1897, and should looted bronzes return?
lesson_6.spokenTitle: Why did Britain invade Benin in 1897, and should looted bronzes return?

cards.heading: 1897 Trade Clash & Invasion
cards.connective: Why did Britain invade Benin in 1897, and should looted bronzes return?
cards.html: Clashing with Oba Ovonramwen over palm oil and rubber, Britain launched the 1897 Punitive Expedition.
cards.spoken: Why did Britain invade Benin in 1897, and should looted bronzes return? <short pause> Clashing with Oba Ovonramwen over palm oil and rubber, Britain launched the 1897 Punitive Expedition.

cards.heading: 4,000+ Looted Bronzes Sold
cards.connective: Soldiers stripped Benin’s sacred visual history archive from the burned palace.
cards.html: Over four thousand artworks from palace storehouses were shipped to London and sold worldwide.
cards.spoken: Soldiers stripped Benin’s sacred visual history archive from the burned palace. <short pause> Over four thousand artworks from palace storehouses were shipped to London and sold worldwide.

cards.heading: Restitution & Living Edo Today
cards.connective: More than a century later, treasures are returning to a thriving royal city.
cards.html: Modern restitution returns bronzes to Nigeria, where Oba Ewuare II and Igun casters thrive today!
cards.spoken: More than a century later, treasures are returning to a thriving royal city. <short pause> Modern restitution returns bronzes to Nigeria, where Oba Ewuare II and Igun casters thrive today!

cards.heading: A Living Thousand-Year Edo Story
cards.connective: From AD 900 Ogiso moats to today’s Igun Street, Edo heritage endures.
cards.html: The Kingdom of Benin shines on through giant Iya walls, lost-wax bronzes, restitution, and living Edo pride.
cards.spoken: From AD 900 Ogiso moats to today’s Igun Street, Edo heritage endures. <short pause> The Kingdom of Benin shines on through giant Iya walls, lost-wax bronzes, restitution, and living Edo pride.

lesson_6.takeaway: After British forces invaded over palm-oil trade in February 1897 and looted 4,000+ bronzes, modern restitution is returning treasures to Nigeria where Oba Ewuare II and Igun Street casters thrive today.
vocab: 1. Oba Ovonramwen
Oba who defended Benin’s independence before exile in 1897.
2. Punitive Expedition
February 1897 British invasion that burned and looted the palace.
3. Looting
Taking sacred art or property by military force in war.
lesson_6.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Ethnologisches Museum Berlin, MARKK Hamburg, MAA Cambridge, National Museum Benin City and Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_6.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> After British forces invaded over palm-oil trade in February 1897 and looted 4,000+ bronzes, modern restitution is returning treasures to Nigeria where Oba Ewuare II and Igun Street casters thrive today.
